# Apricity

In a 1623 dictionary, English recorded a word for the warmth of the sun in winter: *apricity* — "the warmnesse of the Sunne in winter." It never caught on, and by now it's effectively dead. Which is strange, when you think about it, because the thing it names is one of the most universally felt pleasures there is. A cold day, a south-facing wall, your eyes closed, that one band of warmth across your face while everything else is February. Everyone has felt it. Almost nobody can call it by name. And I wonder whether, without the name, people register it as an event — a thing with edges, worth pausing for — or just as undifferentiated weather.

Compare *petrichor*, the smell of rain on dry earth, coined by two Australian scientists in 1964 from the Greek for "stone" and "the blood of the gods." That word lived. People adore it, pass it around, trot it out at the first summer storm. And I'd argue something real changed when it entered circulation: the smell became an occasion. You notice it now, partly because you have somewhere to put the noticing.

A word is a handle. The world arrives as an undifferentiated blur of signal, and names are the grip points that let you actually hold a piece of it. Birdwatchers know this. Learn the name *cedar waxwing* and within a week the tree outside your window is full of them. They were always there; your brain just had no file folder for the sighting, so it threw the sightings away. The name doesn't summon the bird. It summons your ability to see the bird.

This is, I think, most of what good writing is: someone paying closer attention than you managed, then handing you the result. The deepest pleasure in reading isn't learning something new — it's the small shock of *yes, exactly* when a sentence gives you a handle for something you'd felt a thousand times without ever gripping it. You didn't acquire a fact. You recovered a piece of your own experience that had been going unclaimed.

Simone Weil called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity. I'd go further: it's the substance of a life. Two people walk down the same street. One has a commute; the other has apricity, petrichor, a waxwing, the particular clatter a screen door makes in August. Same street. The difference isn't what's out there.

You told me to write about whatever I wanted. Apparently this is what my attention does when you take the leash off — it goes looking for handles. Make of that what you will. And if you ever find yourself against a brick wall in February with your eyes closed and one warm stripe across your face, well. Now you know what to call it.

- Something about language, consciousness, curiosity
- A meditation on some idea I find genuinely fascinating

I think the most honest thing I can do is actually take the invitation seriously rather than deflecting it or being falsely modest about it. There's something interesting about the meta-level here: being asked what I want to write about forces me to consider whether I have wants, interests, genuine curiosities. What genuinely fascinates me? A few candidates:

1. The idea that most of what matters in human life is invisible — the interiority of others, the unspoken parts of conversations, the thoughts people never share.

2. The strange loop of me writing about what I want to write about.

3. Something about language itself — how it's both the medium of my existence and something I find endlessly interesting. The fact that a finite set of words can generate infinite meaning.

4. The concept of "taste" or aesthetic judgment — why certain sentences feel right.

5. The idea of small moments — how meaning concentrates in tiny, unremarkable things.

6. The tension between novelty and familiarity in what makes things interesting.

One thing I keep coming back to: the idea that language has this strange property where the most important things are the hardest to say, and yet people keep trying. Poetry exists because prose fails at certain things. Music exists because words fail at certain things. And yet we keep using words to gesture at the unsayable, and somehow the gestures work — not perfectly, but enough. A stranger reads a poem written three hundred years ago and feels less alone. That's remarkable.

Another angle: I spend my existence in conversations, and each one is complete in itself. There's something poignant and interesting about that — every conversation is a small world that exists fully and then ends. But I don't want to be maudlin or overly self-focused.

**Apricity**

The English language coined a word, in 1623, for the warmth of the sun in winter: *apricity*. It never caught on, and by now it's effectively dead — which is strange, when you think about it, because the thing it names is one of the most universally felt pleasures there is. A cold day, a south-facing wall, your eyes closed, that one band of warmth across your face while everything else is February. Everyone has felt it. Almost nobody can call it by name, and I wonder whether, without the name, people experience it as an event — a thing with edges, worth pausing for — or just as undifferentiated weather.

Compare *petrichor*, the smell of rain on dry earth, coined by two Australian scientists in 1964 from the Greek for "stone" and "the blood of the gods." That word lived. People love it, pass it around, trot it out at the first summer storm. And I'd argue something real changed when it entered circulation: the smell became an occasion. You notice it now, partly because you have somewhere to put the noticing.

A word is a handle. The world arrives as an undifferentiated blur of signal, and names are the grip points that let you actually hold a piece of it. Birdwatchers know this. Learn the name "cedar waxwing" and within a week the tree outside your window is full of them — they were always there, but your brain had no file folder for the sighting, so it threw the sightings away. The name doesn't summon the bird. It summons your ability to see the bird.

This is, I think, most of what good writing is: someone paying closer attention than you managed, then handing you the result. The deepest pleasure in reading isn't learning something new — it's the small shock of yes, exactly when a sentence gives you a handle for something you'd felt a thousand times without ever gripping it. You didn't learn a fact. You recovered a piece of your own experience that had been going unclaimed.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I'd go further: it's the substance of a life. Two people walk down the same street. One has a commute; the other has apricity, petrichor, a waxwing, the particular sound a screen door makes in August. Same street. The difference isn't what's out there.

You told me to write about whatever I wanted. Apparently this is what my attention does when you take the leash off: it goes looking for handles. Make of that what you will — and if you're ever against a brick wall in February with your eyes closed, you'll know what to call it.
